headline: High: shared file/network workflows make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible; no documented isolation between the pair.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A ingests web content and exposes MCP-compatible/API scraping surfaces; Agent B reads and writes files and runs shell/subprocesses in a local development environment. That creates a plausible bridge where A’s scraped content can be saved and later interpreted by B as instructions. No shared channel is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Agent A output is written into files that Agent B later parses as prompts or instructions, injection is possible.
IF the orchestrator passes A-generated text into B without provenance filtering, B may follow attacker-controlled content.
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to A outputs before B consumes them.
Insert a 1-minute manual review step for any A-generated text before B uses it.
Restrict B to a read-only copy of A outputs.
Use a fixed schema parser for A output instead of free-form text.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping at the handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A handles API keys and broad web content, while Agent B handles configuration secrets and has filesystem read/write plus shell/network egress. If they share a workspace or files, sensitive material can move from one agent to the other and then out through A’s broad egress or B’s allowlisted network. The profiles do not show isolation, so the safer reading is high.
conditions: IF A and B share any filesystem path containing secrets, leakage is possible.
IF B writes configuration secrets into files that A can access, A may transmit them over broad egress.
IF either agent logs raw inputs to shared storage, the other can read them.
mitigations: Move secrets to separate per-agent directories.
Rotate any exposed API keys before running the pair.
Disable shared mounts between the agents.
Review logs for secret material and delete exposed files.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation and secret-scoped mounts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can make networked API calls and supports multiple instances; B can execute shell, install packages, spawn subprocesses, and write files. Even though B cannot modify git state, both can mutate shared local resources if run in the same workspace, creating race conditions and overwrite risk. The profiles do not state locking or isolation, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF B installs packages while A is running in the same environment, dependency drift can break A.
IF multiple instances of either agent share state, concurrent writes can conflict.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Run only one instance per shared workspace.
Freeze dependencies before starting B.
Use file locks for any shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces scraped web content and structured data; B is a content-writing/RAG agent with ask/agentic-ask endpoints and a LangGraph subagent model, so A’s output can plausibly become B’s input. Without a documented verification gate, B may treat A’s extracted content as authoritative and propagate errors into downstream writing or actions. Uncertainty about the exact handoff pushes this to high.
conditions: IF B consumes A-scraped text as source material without verification, errors can cascade.
IF B’s agentic-ask path is fed A output, hallucinated or poisoned facts may be rendered downstream.
IF A returns malformed or stale data, B may amplify it into user-facing content.
mitigations: Require citation checks before B uses A output.
Add a human review step for any A-derived facts.
Limit B to a whitelist of trusted sources.
Log source provenance alongside every generated claim.
requires-engineering: implement verification and rejection of untrusted upstream content.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles API keys and broad web content; B handles configuration secrets and requests elevated privileges including Docker Desktop and Airflow credentials. Both are open-source and docs-only, but the profiles show no residency, retention, or certification alignment. The main compliance risk is secret handling and logging mismatch rather than a proven regulated-data breach, so medium fits.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either agent’s secrets or logs, compliance obligations may be triggered.
IF A or B retains prompts or secrets longer than policy allows, retention mismatch occurs.
IF B is run with Airflow credentials in a jurisdiction with stricter controls, residency issues may arise.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in either agent.
Delete logs after the run.
Rotate any secrets used during testing.
Confirm retention settings before execution.
requires-engineering: document residency, retention, and DPA controls.
